1.q: אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה כִּ֣י דִלִּיתָ֑⁠נִי וְ⁠לֹא־שִׂמַּ֖חְתָּ אֹיְבַ֣⁠י לִֽ⁠י
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you, Yahweh] or [Yahweh, because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you]
If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put **Yahweh** at the beginning of this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I will extol you for you have drawn me up]

Here David is speaking of God’s help as if God had physically raised him up from a lower place to a higher place. The other times the word the ULT translates as **have drawn me up** occurs in the Old Testament, it refers to drawing water out of a well with a bucket. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have helped me] or [you have delivered me]

2.note: David is not using the phrase **my God** to mean that he is the only one who worships Yahweh nor that he possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God that he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, Yahweh, God whom I worship,]

3.note: The word **Sheol** refers to the place of the dead, where dead people go, and the word **pit** also refers to the grave. These two phrases, **you have brought up my soul from Sheol** and **you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit**, mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [you have brought up my soul from Sheol, yes, you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit]
David is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have brought me up]

David assumes that readers will know that **the pit** refers to the grave or death. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the ones going down to death] or [from the ones going down to the grave]

4.q: זַמְּר֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה חֲסִידָ֑י⁠ו וְ֝⁠הוֹד֗וּ לְ⁠זֵ֣כֶר קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ׃ כִּ֤י רֶ֨גַע ׀ בְּ⁠אַפּ⁠וֹ֮ חַיִּ֪ים בִּ⁠רְצ֫וֹנ֥⁠וֹ בָּ֭⁠עֶרֶב יָלִ֥ין בֶּ֗כִי וְ⁠לַ⁠בֹּ֥קֶר רִנָּֽה
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of verse 4 and the first half of verse 5, since the first half of verse 5 gives the reason for the result that verse 4 describes. Alternate translation: [Because his anger is {for} a moment, {but} his favor is {for} a lifetime, sing praise to Yahweh, {you} his faithful ones, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **remembrance** and **holiness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Here the phrase **his holiness** refers to Yahweh’s holy character and the actions that he had done in the past as a result of his holy character. Alternate translation: [when you remember how holy he is and the great things that he has done as a result]

5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger** and **favor**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [For he is angry only for a moment, but he shows kindness for a lifetime]

David is using **a moment** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a very short time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his anger is for a brief time] or [his anger is only temporary]

David is speaking of **weeping** and **rejoicing** as if they were living things that could come to a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the evening people may weep, but in the morning people will rejoice]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **ease**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when my life was easy]

The expression **I will never be shaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing will ever shake me] or [I will always remain secure]

David is speaking of himself as if he were an object that could not be**shaken** (physically moved or disturbed). He means that he felt completely secure and believed nothing could threaten his stability or well-being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will always be secure] or [nothing will ever threaten me]

7.note: See how you translated the word **favor** in 30:5.

The phrase **you have made my mountain stand strong** could be: (1) David speaking of his security and strength as if they were **my mountain**. Alternate translation: [you have made me as secure as a mountain] or [you have given me great strength and security] (2) David using the phrase **my mountain** to refer to Mount Zion in which case David would be using Mount Zion to represent his rule as king which he would do from Mount Zion. Alternate translation: [you have made my reign secure] or [you have firmly established my rule]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [then you hid your face from me]

Here, **your face** represents Yahweh’s presence or attention (and consequently also some of the help or protection that would have come as a result). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you withdrew your presence from me] or [you turned your attention away from me]

8.note: See how you translated the word **favor** in 30:5.

9.q: מַה־בֶּ֥צַע בְּ⁠דָמִ⁠י֮ בְּ⁠רִדְתִּ֪⁠י אֶ֫ל־שָׁ֥חַת הֲ⁠יוֹדְ⁠ךָ֥ עָפָ֑ר הֲ⁠יַגִּ֥יד אֲמִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ׃ שְׁמַע־יְהוָ֥ה וְ⁠חָנֵּ֑⁠נִי יְ֝הוָה הֱֽיֵה־עֹזֵ֥ר לִֽ⁠י
9.note: This is the beginning of what David said or prayed to Yahweh. The ULT indicates the beginning and end of David’s direct address of Yahweh with quotation marks and the UST introduces David’s words with the phrase “I said.” Consider natural ways of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [I prayed, “What profit is there…”]

9.q: מַה־בֶּ֥צַע בְּ⁠דָמִ⁠י֮ בְּ⁠רִדְתִּ֪⁠י אֶ֫ל־שָׁ֥חַת הֲ⁠יוֹדְ⁠ךָ֥ עָפָ֑ר הֲ⁠יַגִּ֥יד אֲמִתֶּֽ⁠ךָ
9.note: David is using a question to emphasize that his death would not benefit God and to make the point that dead people cannot praise God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for this purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [There is no profit in my blood, in my descent to the pit. The dust will not praise you! It will not declare your faithfulness!]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. [What advantage is there in my death, yes, in my going down to the grave]
Here, **blood** represents “death.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my death]

David assumes that readers will know that **the pit** refers to the dwelling place of the dead. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. (In 30:3 David uses a different Hebrew word for “pit,” but there the word has the same meaning as it does here so you could see how you translated “pit” there.) Alternate translation: [to the place of the dead] or [to the abode of the dead]

Here, **dust** represents those who are dead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Will those who are dead praise you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way as in the UST.

10.note: Here, **Hear** represents “Listen and respond.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Listen to me and respond] or [Pay attention to me]

David is using imperative forms, but he is communicating polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms **Hear**, **be gracious to me**, and **be my helper** do not communicate polite requests in your language, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please hear, Yahweh, and please be gracious to me. Yahweh, please be my helper]

11.note: David assumes that readers will know **sackcloth** was a coarse material worn as a sign of mourning or distress. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have removed my mourning clothes and have clothed me with gladness]

Here, **gladness** represents clothing that was worn for joyous occasions that would express gladness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with celebratory clothes] or [with clothes worn to celebrate]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and have covered me with clothes that show that I am glad] or [and have clothed me with celebratory clothes]

12.note: Here, **so that** marks **my glory may sing praise to you and not be silent** as the goal or purpose of “You have turned for me, my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and have clothed me with gladness” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for the purpose that] or [to the end that]

By **my glory**, David probably means some part of his inner being that represented where his honor was. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [my soul may sing praise to you] or [I may sing praise to you]

David is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather, David is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God I worship]
